```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidymodels)
library(tidyverse)
source(here::here("R/theme.R"))
source(here::here("R/data.R"))
```

## A lot compared with what

"Neural networks need a lot of data" is the standard caution, and it is repeated so often
that it has stopped carrying any information. A lot compared with what? Ten thousand rows?
A million? Marine surveys are usually in the hundreds, so the question is not academic: it
decides whether the method is available to you at all.

This page measures it, on a survey of exactly the size most of us actually have.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

## The setup

Eight predictors, 720 stations with complete records, and a fixed 160-station test set that
no model is ever fitted on. We draw training sets of increasing size from the remaining 560
and watch the test RMSE fall. Fifteen draws at each size, so that the spread is visible as
well as the mean.

```{r}
#| label: setup-data
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean()

modelling <- survey |>
  select(station_id, abundance, depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3,
         salinity_psu, substrate, season, longitude, latitude) |>
  drop_na() |>
  inner_join(load_coastal_survey_truth(), by = "station_id")

set.seed(99)
test_rows <- sample(nrow(modelling), 160)
test <- modelling[test_rows, ]
pool <- modelling[-test_rows, ]

base_recipe <- recipe(abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 +
                        salinity_psu + substrate + season + longitude + latitude,
                      data = pool) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

c(pool = nrow(pool), test = nrow(test))
```

Two reference points matter more than any of the models, and both are worth computing
before you fit anything.

```{r}
#| label: reference-points
tibble(reference = c("predict the mean of the training pool",
                     "predict the true expected count (oracle)"),
       `test RMSE` = round(c(rmse_vec(test$abundance, rep(mean(pool$abundance), nrow(test))),
                             rmse_vec(test$abundance, test$true_mean)), 3))
```

The mean-only baseline scores 4.402. A model that knows the exact expected count at every
station, the quantity the simulation drew from and available to us only because we wrote the
simulation, scores 3.701. **Everything any method could ever learn lives in that gap of
0.70 RMSE.** The rest is negative-binomial sampling noise and no amount of data removes it.

That number reframes the whole page. We are not asking whether a network can learn; we are
asking how much of a 0.70 window it can claim.

## Worked example: the learning curves

Four models. A linear model, a random forest, a neural network with eight hidden units,
the sort of configuration you would write without thinking, and a second network with the
configuration that ten-fold cross-validation on the full dataset actually chose, which we
come back to below.

```{r}
#| label: learning-curves
specs <- list(
  `linear regression`        = linear_reg(),
  `random forest`            = rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
                                 set_engine("ranger", seed = 1) |> set_mode("regression"),
  `neural network (8 units)` = mlp(hidden_units = 8, penalty = 0.01, epochs = 400) |>
                                 set_engine("nnet") |> set_mode("regression"),
  `neural network (tuned)`   = mlp(hidden_units = 1, penalty = 1, epochs = 400) |>
                                 set_engine("nnet") |> set_mode("regression")
)

sizes <- c(40, 80, 160, 320, 480)

curves <- map_dfr(1:15, \(replicate) {
  map_dfr(sizes, \(n) {
    set.seed(1000 * replicate + n)
    training <- pool[sample(nrow(pool), n), ]
    map_dfr(names(specs), \(nm) {
      set.seed(7)
      fitted <- fit(workflow() |> add_recipe(base_recipe) |> add_model(specs[[nm]]), training)
      tibble(replicate = replicate, n = n, model = nm,
             rmse = rmse_vec(test$abundance, predict(fitted, test)$.pred))
    })
  })
})

curves |>
  summarise(`mean RMSE` = round(mean(rmse), 2), `sd across draws` = round(sd(rmse), 2),
            .by = c(n, model)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = c(`mean RMSE`, `sd across draws`)) |>
  select(n, starts_with("mean")) |>
  rename_with(\(x) str_remove(x, "mean RMSE_")) |>
  arrange(n)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-learning-curves
#| fig-cap: "Test RMSE against training-set size, fifteen draws at each size, on a fixed 160-station test set. Ribbons span the tenth to ninetieth percentile of the draws and are clipped at the top of the panel. The upper dashed line is the mean-only baseline; the lower one is the oracle that knows each station's true expected count. Only the band between them is learnable."
#| fig-alt: "Four lines, each with a shaded ribbon spanning the tenth to ninetieth percentile of fifteen draws, against training-set size on a log-scaled axis. The random forest line is lowest throughout with the narrowest ribbon, falling from about 4.45 at forty stations to about 3.97 at four hundred and eighty. Linear regression starts at about 6.06 with a very wide ribbon, drops steeply to 4.82 by eighty stations and flattens near 4.20. The tuned network starts lower at about 5.31, crosses linear regression twice and ends just below it at about 4.09. The eight-unit network is far above the others at every size, rising to about 7.8 at eighty stations before falling to about 5.26, and its ribbon is the widest on the plot, running off the top of the panel across most of the range; it never crosses the upper dashed line. Two horizontal dashed lines mark 4.40, labelled predict the mean, and 3.70, labelled oracle."
#| fig-width: 7.8
#| fig-height: 4.8
baseline <- rmse_vec(test$abundance, rep(mean(pool$abundance), nrow(test)))
oracle   <- rmse_vec(test$abundance, test$true_mean)

curves |>
  summarise(lower = quantile(rmse, 0.1), upper = quantile(rmse, 0.9), rmse = mean(rmse),
            .by = c(n, model)) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, rmse, colour = model, fill = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(baseline, oracle), linetype = "dashed", colour = "#9aa5ad") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = sizes) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(3.5, 8.2)) +
  annotate("text", x = 40, y = baseline, label = "predict the mean", hjust = 0, vjust = -0.6,
           size = 3.2, colour = "#77818a") +
  annotate("text", x = 40, y = oracle, label = "oracle", hjust = 0, vjust = -0.6,
           size = 3.2, colour = "#77818a") +
  labs(x = "training stations (log scale)", y = "test RMSE", colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2), fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

Read the upper dashed line first. **At 40 stations, every method except the random forest
is worse than predicting the mean**, and the linear model is the worst of all at 6.06,
because thirteen coefficients on forty rows is a fit to nothing. That is not a fact about
neural networks. It is what small data does to every flexible method.

Now the eight-unit network. It is above the baseline at every size, and at 480 stations it
still scores 5.26 against the baseline's 4.402, and the spread across draws is enormous,
with a standard deviation of 1.70 at 80 stations. Its curve is not even monotone: it is
*worse* at 80 stations than at 40. With 113 weights and a penalty of 0.01 it is not
learning, it is thrashing, and a single run of it would have given you a number with no
information in it whatsoever.

## The configuration the search chose

Before concluding anything about networks, we owe the method a fair configuration. Here is
what ten-fold cross-validation picks when allowed to search.

```{r}
#| label: tuning
tunable <- mlp(hidden_units = tune(), penalty = tune(), epochs = 500) |>
  set_engine("nnet") |> set_mode("regression")

set.seed(11)
folds <- vfold_cv(modelling, v = 10)

set.seed(12)
searched <- tune_grid(
  workflow() |> add_recipe(base_recipe) |> add_model(tunable),
  resamples = folds,
  grid = expand_grid(hidden_units = c(1, 2, 4, 8, 16), penalty = c(0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1)),
  metrics = metric_set(rmse)
)

show_best(searched, metric = "rmse", n = 5) |>
  select(hidden_units, penalty, mean, std_err) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

The search chose **one hidden unit with a penalty of 1**, the most heavily restricted
network on the grid, and the one closest to a linear model. Asked how much nonlinearity
this dataset could support, cross-validation answered: almost none.

That configuration is the fourth line on @fig-learning-curves, and it behaves sensibly. It
tracks linear regression from 160 stations onwards and edges past it at 480 (4.09 against
4.20). It is a perfectly respectable model. It is also, on this data, a linear model with
extra steps.

The random forest wins at every size, ending at 3.97, about 64% of the way from the
baseline to the oracle floor.

## The diagnostic that explains it

The obvious conclusion is "the network needed more rows". That conclusion is wrong, and we
can show it is wrong, because we have the true expected count for every station.

Refit everything with `true_mean` as the target instead of `abundance`. Same predictors,
same sizes, same code: the only change is that the negative-binomial noise has been
removed from what the model is asked to predict.

::: {.callout-warning}
This is a **diagnostic, not a model**. No real dataset has a noise-free target, and an RMSE
computed against `true_mean` is not achievable in practice. We use it here for the one
thing it is good for: separating "the model could not learn the signal" from "the signal is
buried in noise".
:::

```{r}
#| label: noise-free
truth_recipe <- recipe(true_mean ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 +
                         salinity_psu + substrate + season + longitude + latitude,
                       data = pool) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

noise_free <- map_dfr(1:10, \(replicate) {
  map_dfr(c(80, 320, 480), \(n) {
    set.seed(1000 * replicate + n)
    training <- pool[sample(nrow(pool), n), ]
    map_dfr(names(specs)[1:3], \(nm) {
      set.seed(7)
      fitted <- fit(workflow() |> add_recipe(truth_recipe) |> add_model(specs[[nm]]), training)
      tibble(n = n, model = nm,
             rmse = rmse_vec(test$true_mean, predict(fitted, test)$.pred))
    })
  })
})

noise_free |>
  summarise(rmse = round(mean(rmse), 2), .by = c(n, model)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = rmse) |>
  arrange(n)
```

The ordering reverses. Against the noise-free signal the eight-unit network beats linear
regression from 320 stations onwards, and by 480 it is at 1.88 against the linear model's
2.47, or **24% better**. Linear regression has stopped improving; it is at its ceiling,
because it cannot represent the two humped responses that are actually in the generator.
The network can, and did.

So the network did learn the structure. It learned it well, on a few hundred rows. Then
negative-binomial noise was added on top, and on the observed counts that advantage
disappeared and reversed.

## Rows per unit of signal

**The requirement is not rows. It is rows per unit of signal.** A network is a
high-variance estimator: it has many parameters, the loss surface is not convex, and
different draws give different answers. That variance has to be paid for out of the signal
available, and on this survey there is only 0.70 RMSE of signal to pay with. A random
forest, which averages 500 trees and is therefore much lower variance, pays the bill
comfortably. A linear model, with thirteen parameters and no flexibility to misuse, also
pays it. The network cannot.

The practical rule that follows is the honest version of "networks need a lot of data":

> Before reaching for a network, estimate your baseline and your ceiling. If a
> no-skill baseline and the best imaginable model are close together, the extra flexibility
> has nothing to buy and a great deal to lose.

You will not have an oracle. But you usually have something: the repeatability of duplicate
tows, the variance between replicate grabs, the agreement between two observers. Any of
those estimates the noise floor, and any of them is more informative about whether a
network is worth trying than the row count is.

## Limits of this comparison

**This is one dataset with one noise structure.** Counts with a negative-binomial dispersion
of 1.5 are about as noisy as marine data gets. On a well-measured continuous response, such as a
CTD-derived variable or a stable acoustic index, the signal fraction is far higher and the
conclusions would shift towards the flexible methods.

**Eight predictors is a small table.** The network's advantage grows with the number of
inputs that interact, and eight additive-ish columns is the case least favourable to it.
[The last page of this section](when-to-use-one.qmd) constructs the favourable case.

**We tuned two hyperparameters, not four.** A more careful search over the learning rate
and epochs might do better. It would also, as §7 insisted, have to sit inside the resampling
to be honest about it, and the search itself would cost more than the model is worth here.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key points

- **Compute your baseline and your ceiling first.** On this survey they are 4.402 and
  3.701, so everything any method can ever learn is a 0.70 window in RMSE.
- **At 40 training stations every flexible method loses to predicting the mean.** The
  linear model with thirteen coefficients was the worst of all.
- A default eight-unit network never beat the mean-only baseline at any size, and varied by
  a standard deviation of 1.70 between draws of the same size.
- **Cross-validation tuned the network down to one hidden unit and a penalty of 1**,
  almost a linear model, and then it performed like one.
- **The network was not short of rows; it was short of signal.** On the noise-free target
  it beat linear regression by 24% at 480 stations. The flexibility was real. The noise
  buried it.
:::

## Try it yourself

1. Rerun the learning curves with `abundance` replaced by the binary `present` column and
   RMSE by `roc_auc`. Presence is a less noisy summary than the count: does the ordering
   of the four models change?
2. Add a fifth model: `mlp(hidden_units = 8, penalty = 1)`. How much of the eight-unit
   network's terrible performance was the width, and how much was the missing penalty?
